newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian markets wary as Mahathir plans long break.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian markets wary as Mahathir plans long break.

text.p: Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's plan to take an unusually long two-month break has unnerved Malaysian markets which have memories of mishaps during the premier's past absences.

As word first leaked out on Wednesday that the hyperkinetic prime minister was going on a lengthy break beginning May 19, the foreign exchange market was the first to react, with the ringgit losing some 80 basis points, to end at 2.5125/35 to the dollar that day.
Mahathir confirmed on Thursday that he will visit Britain and Eastern Europe on a work-and-rest mission, leaving Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim fully in charge.

While Anwar has functioned as a stand-in during shorter Mahathir absences, the unprecedented length of the leave generated worries -- some real, some overblown and others artificially created, financial analysts and dealers said.
A stockbroker at a leading bank-owned brokerage said, "With him away, now and then there'll be problems, so people will be cautious."
At Friday's close, the blue chip stock market barometer, the Composite Index, was up 0.23 points points or 0.02 percent, to 1,107.37.
On Friday, the ringgit rebounded, and was at 2.5070/75 at 0940 GMT. Malaysia's financial markets were closed on Thursday for a Moslem holiday.
But the calm in Kuala Lumpur's markets belies a tendency by Malaysian investors to rely on rumours and theories rather than hard news or government pronouncements, analysts said.
The vacation news raised questions about the country's stability, the premiership succession and Mahathir's health, market players said.
In the recent past, Mahathir's absence has coincided with a number of negative developments.

Market players recalled that the last time Mahathir was away in Japan in March, Malaysia's relationship with Singapore soured over unflattering comments about Malaysia's Johor state by Singapore Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew.

Other market-jarring events while Mahathir was away include the ugly break-up of a conference about East Timor in Kuala Lumpur last November and last June's declaration that the huge Bakun dam project on Borneo Island violated environmental laws.
But Mahathir said he did not expect any problems during his absence. "I don't foresee any major disasters with our nation or with our neighbours," he said.

"Anwar no doubt may be unhappy with the markets' lack of confidence in him. Thus the deputy PM will want to convince investors of his ability to lead," said Jimmy Koh, economist at market research firm I.D.E.A.
There were also some worries that 71-year old Mahathir, who had a heart operation eight years ago, may be going away for secret health checks, market players said.
"I think the worry is that he is going away for another heart bypass," said a manager at a European investment house.
Mahathir had a heart operation eight years ago.
But Mahathir firmly denied there were any health problems.

Some analysts said the handing over of power -- the first time in 12 years that Mahathir will formally appoint his deputy as acting premier -- is a sign of Mahathir's confidence in Anwar, rather than a test of Anwar's ability.
"I don't think he has to test his deputy. He should know what the man is capable of by now," political commentator Rustam Sani told Reuters.
